c.tagline: Glamour, grand prix, and grand hotels crowded onto a single Riviera cliff.

taxi.fareNote: Metered within Monaco; fixed rates typically apply for transfers to/from Nice Airport.

emergency.note: Monaco uses the same emergency numbers as France; 112 works for all emergencies from any phone. Princess Grace Hospital (Centre Hospitalier Princesse Grace, CHPG) is the main medical facility.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing is rare but possible in Grand Prix and casino-district crowds.

hood_desc: The glamorous heart of Monaco around the famous casino, with grand Belle Époque palace hotels, designer boutiques, and the F1 circuit; best for travelers chasing luxury, nightlife, and glitz.

The harborfront district around Port Hercule with the daily market, marina-view cafes, the train station, and a more local, walkable feel; suits visitors wanting a central but slightly less flashy base.
A modern district built on reclaimed land around the marina, with parks, the Stade Louis II, and the heliport; calmer and greener, good for families or those wanting some breathing room.
Monaco's beach district along Avenue Princesse Grace with the Japanese Garden and beach clubs facing the Mediterranean; ideal for sun-seekers and resort-style stays.
A French hillside town literally across the street from the Casino de Monte-Carlo, offering noticeably cheaper lodging within a short walk of Monaco's sights; best for budget-conscious travelers.

water.note: Meets strict EU standards and is safe to drink, with only a mild chlorine taste.

transit.pay: CAM bus fares are paid by tapping a contactless bank card directly on board, using a prepaid CAM card, or via the CAM mobile app; single tickets can also be bought at onboard machines. The little Bateau Bus shuttle across Port Hercule is free to ride.
transit.hours: CAM buses run roughly 7am-9pm with reduced evening frequency; there is no dedicated night-bus network, so taxis fill the gap late at night.
transit.note: Monaco is compact enough to explore mostly on foot, aided by a dense network of public elevators and escalators that help with the steep terrain between quarters.

train: Monaco-Monte-Carlo station (mainline SNCF/TER service linking Nice and Ventimiglia)
bus: Zou! regional buses to Nice, Menton and nearby towns

airport.name: Nice Côte d'Azur Airport (NCE)
airport.drive: 30-45 min by car/taxi along the coast (A8 motorway or coastal roads), longer in heavy traffic

transit.m: Train to Nice-Ville then transfer to airport bus/tram (~40 min total)

tip.r: A 15% service charge is included by law in restaurant and hotel bills (service compris); rounding up or leaving a few extra euros for good service is appreciated but not required.

food.name: Barbagiuan
food.desc: Monaco's national snack: little fried pastry parcels stuffed with Swiss chard, ricotta, onion and parmesan, eaten hot as a starter or street bite.

places.name: U Cavagnetu
places.note: Family-run Monegasque bistro in the old town whose barbagiuan is its signature.

places.name: Marche de la Condamine
places.note: Halle Gourmande counters sell barbagiuan by the piece at everyday prices.

places.name: Castelroc
places.note: Long-standing address for Monegasque classics served on a shaded terrace.

food.name: Socca
food.desc: Thin chickpea-flour pancake baked blistering hot in a copper pan, scraped onto paper and eaten with black pepper and your fingers.

places.name: Chez Roger
places.note: Market stall turning out socca hot from the oven, a lunchtime fixture for locals.

places.name: Marche de la Condamine
places.note: Several counters in the covered hall serve socca alongside fresh pasta and pissaladiere.

places.name: Maison Multari
places.note: Riviera bakery chain doing socca and pan bagnat for a quick, cheap lunch.

food.name: Stocafi
food.desc: Slow-cooked stockfish stew, the dried cod simmered for hours in tomato, black olives, garlic and herbs. The most old-school Monegasque plate.

places.name: Castelroc
places.note: Known for keeping the traditional stocafi recipe on the menu year round.

places.name: U Cavagnetu
places.note: Home-style Monegasque cooking, stocafi among the daily specials.

places.name: La Montgolfiere
places.note: Husband-and-wife bistro from the Geraci family with a Monegasque-leaning menu.

food.name: Fougasse monegasque
food.desc: Sweet flat bread perfumed with orange-flower water and anise, studded with nuts and scattered with red and white sugared aniseed for the national colours.

places.name: Marche de la Condamine
places.note: Bakery stalls in the market keep the sugared national fougasse in stock.

places.name: Maison Multari
places.note: Local bakery selling sweet fougasse alongside Riviera breads and tarts.

places.name: Boulangeries of Monaco-Ville
places.note: Old-town bakeries near the Palace sell the fougasse whole or by the slice.

food.name: Tourte de blettes
food.desc: Riviera chard tart that comes both ways: savoury with cheese and pine nuts, or sweet with raisins, apple and a dusting of icing sugar.

places.name: Marche de la Condamine
places.note: Traiteur counters cut the chard tart by the slice, sweet and savoury versions.

places.name: U Cavagnetu
places.note: Traditional kitchen where the tart appears as starter or dessert.

places.name: Castelroc
places.note: Regional menu that regularly includes the chard tart among Monegasque plates.

food.name: Pissaladiere
food.desc: Ligurian-Nicoise onion tart on bread dough, the slow-melted onions lattice-topped with anchovy fillets and small black olives.

places.name: Marche de la Condamine
places.note: Sold hot by the square at the market bakery counters through the morning.

places.name: Maison Multari
places.note: Reliable bakery version to eat standing or take to the port.

places.name: Old-town bakeries, rue Comte Felix Gastaldi
places.note: Small shops on the Rock selling pissaladiere and socca slices to walkers.

food.name: Brasserie de Monaco beer
food.desc: Unfiltered lagers and ales brewed in the Principality itself, poured fresh at the brewery tanks on the port.

places.name: Brasserie de Monaco
places.note: Monaco's own microbrewery and taproom, brewing on site overlooking the harbour.

places.name: Stars'N'Bars
places.note: Casual quayside bar stocking the local brews without Monte-Carlo prices.

places.name: Quai des Artistes
places.note: Brasserie on the harbour front pairing local beer with Riviera plates.

food.name: Un Monaco
food.desc: The drink that carries the name: light beer topped with lemonade and a shot of grenadine, pink, low-strength and made for hot afternoons.

places.name: Cafe de Paris Monte-Carlo
places.note: Grand terrace opposite the Casino, the classic spot for an afternoon drink.

places.name: Brasserie de Monaco
places.note: Mixes the Monaco with its own beer, on the terrace by the yachts.

places.name: Stars'N'Bars
places.note: Easy-going port bar; a cheap Monaco with a harbour view.

landmarks: Prince's Palace of Monaco
The official residence of Monaco's ruling family, perched on the Rock with sweeping Mediterranean views and a daily changing of the guard.
Monte Carlo Casino
The opulent Belle Époque gambling house that epitomizes Monaco's glamour, immortalized in film and postcards alike.
Monaco Cathedral
A Romanesque-Byzantine cathedral overlooking the sea, the resting place of Grace Kelly and Monaco's princes.
Oceanographic Museum of Monaco
A dramatic cliffside museum and aquarium founded by Prince Albert I, blending marine science with stunning architecture.
Monte Carlo Casino Square (Place du Casino)
The glitzy plaza in front of the casino, ringed by luxury hotels and often filled with parked supercars.
Larvotto Beach
Monaco's main public beach, a small sandy stretch on the Mediterranean popular for swimming and sunbathing.
Circuit de Monaco (Monaco Grand Prix track)
The legendary narrow street circuit through Monte Carlo that hosts Formula 1's most glamorous race.
Port Hercules
Monaco's deep-water marina crowded with luxury yachts, offering a classic postcard view of the principality.
Exotic Garden of Monaco (Jardin Exotique)
A cliffside garden of cacti and succulents offering panoramic views over Monaco and the sea below.
Saint Martin Gardens
Scenic seaside gardens near the Oceanographic Museum with winding paths and dramatic coastal cliff views.

train.note: Monaco has no railway of its own - the single Monaco-Monte-Carlo station is operated by French SNCF, and frequent coastal TER trains are the way in and out. There is no direct TGV to Paris: change at Nice (about 6h30 total).

bus.note: No long-distance international coaches start in Monaco - the nearest FlixBus and BlaBlaCar Bus hub is Nice. Regional Zou! buses and trains link Monaco with Nice, Menton and the nearby Italian border towns.

ferry.note: No scheduled passenger ferries serve Monaco - Port Hercule handles yachts and cruise-ship calls only. The nearest ferry port is Nice, where Corsica Ferries sails to Corsica.

half.name: Nice
half.blurb: People stroll the Promenade des Anglais, explore the old town and browse its lively markets.

half.name: Eze
half.blurb: This medieval hilltop village charms visitors with stone lanes and sweeping views over the sea.

half.name: Menton
half.blurb: Known as the pearl of France, it draws people with pastel houses, gardens and lemon groves.

half.name: Villefranche-sur-Mer
half.blurb: A picturesque fishing harbor with a colorful old town and one of the coast's prettiest bays.

half.name: Antibes
half.blurb: Visitors wander the ramparts, the market and the Picasso Museum in its atmospheric old town.

half.name: Cannes
half.blurb: Famous for its film festival, glamorous beaches and the palm-lined La Croisette boulevard.
